8a52f1ecaec07c6d: WASHINGTON: An Iowa judge, citing First Amendment protections, dismissed President Donald Trump's lawsuit filed in late 2024 against the Des Moines Register newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer over a poll that showed the Republican leader trailing before the 2024 elections.

"At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability," Iowa District Judge Scott Beattie said in the ruling on Wednesday.
Trump, who has repeatedly clashed with the media in and outside of court, won the 2024 election.

The ruling in the Register case came as another judge told a hearing that Trump's decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House did not appear to comply with prior rulings by a federal appellate court.
Trump had criticised a poll published on Nov 2, 2024, that showed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris leading him by three percentage points in Iowa.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Wednesday ruling.
Free speech group FIRE, which represented Selzer, welcomed the ruling.

"We're pleased that the court recognised what we've said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought," FIRE chief counsel Bob Corn-Revere said in a statement.

Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop news programmes he dislikes, called on the Federal Communications Commission to strip disfavoured broadcast stations of their licences, filed several lawsuits against media outlets and banned some media outlets from the White House.
The US Constitution's First Amendment grants protections for free speech and a free press.

a576280c978c4c36: PETALING JAYA: An analyst sees Pejuang as being at a crossroads of sorts in the wake of former prime minister Najib Razak’s conditional pardon and the manner in which its fellow Perikatan Nasional partners have welcomed it.

Asrul Hadi, associate vice-president at The Asia Group, said Pejuang faced a test of its principles concerning its relatively new PN membership, having been a vocal critic of Najib and championing itself as a party at the forefront of the fight against corruption.
Asrul said opposition to Najib and the political culture linked to the 1MDB scandal was fundamental to Pejuang’s formation, setting it apart from other Malay-based parties.

“If Pejuang dilutes its anti-corruption position simply to retain access to PN’s machinery, it may survive organisationally but become politically irrelevant because voters will no longer understand what it represents,” he told FMT.
Asrul acknowledged that Pejuang, which was formed by former prime minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad in 2021, was already weak, and that leaving PN risked inviting political irrelevance.
However, he said the PN it had joined was not the same entity led by Bersatu president Muhyiddin Yassin, with PAS now in the driver’s seat and appearing increasingly Najib- and Umno-friendly.
Prolonged ambiguity over the matter could alienate some of Pejuang’s already few leaders and members, he warned.

Asrul also said there might be little space for Pejuang under a PN-Barisan Nasional pact, given that any electoral arrangement would prioritise Umno, PAS and opposition leader Hamzah Zainudin’s Wawasan.
“Umno has the established Malay nationalist brand and machinery, PAS has the grassroots network, and Hamzah’s Wawasan brings elected representatives and former Bersatu networks.

“Pejuang risks being treated as a peripheral partner. It must decide whether access to PN’s electoral machinery is worth the erosion of its identity and whether PN’s principal actors believe they need Pejuang at all.”

Under the conditional pardon for his SRC International conviction, Najib will be allowed to serve the remainder of his jail term at home if he pays his RM50 million fine, an already reduced amount from the initial RM210 million fine.

Umno has launched a fund to help its former president settle the fine, while PAS said it believed Najib could contribute to the country even while he remained under house arrest. Wawasan said it was grateful the decision had put an end to the polemic surrounding Najib’s pardon.

However, Pejuang information chief Rafique Rashid Ali called for clarity on the mechanism and conditions for inmates to be granted house arrests, warning against only allowing this arrangement for elites.
Asrul described Rafique’s statement as “careful”, subtly asserting Pejuang’s position on Najib without questioning the king’s constitutional power to pardon or directly confronting PAS and Umno.

“He may also be testing how much room Pejuang has to retain an independent identity within PN. Eventually, however, the party must show whether it will defend that position when doing so carries a real political cost.”
Pragmatism and survival more essential
However, Universiti Sains Malaysia’s Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid said Pejuang needed to be more pragmatic about the matter, pointing out that the party’s long-term relevance and existence were at stake.

Remaining in PN could allow Pejuang to win a couple of seats in Parliament, he said, and even possibly a spot in the Cabinet if the coalition went on to form and lead the government after the next general election.
He added that all these factors determined a party’s sustainability and relevance.
Fauzi said Pejuang could opt to take a more principled stand on Najib and corruption in general in internal discussions within PN.

“Pejuang’s presence in PN may also prove crucial to the coalition as it shows PN’s internal democracy by tolerating dissent. Plus, not all in PN would tolerate BN’s mollycoddling of Najib, even as BN’s relationship with PN grows closer.”
He added that Rafique’s statement was unlikely to affect ties with PAS or Umno, as Mukhriz Mahathir was Pejuang’s president and had not touched on Najib’s pardon.
“So long as Mukhriz is silent on the matter, they shouldn’t suspect that Pejuang might be interested in stepping out of PN’s official line as yet,” he added.
64a6df66bc10914e: PETALING JAYA: Seorang penganalisis melihat Pejuang seolah-olah berada di persimpangan susulan pengampunan bersyarat diberikan kepada bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak serta cara rakan sekutunya dalam Perikatan Nasional (PN) menyambut keputusan itu.

Asrul Hadi, naib presiden bersekutu di The Asia Group berkata Pejuang kini berdepan ujian untuk mempertahankan prinsipnya sebagai anggota baharu PN, selepas lantang mengkritik Najib serta tampil sebagai parti yang menentang rasuah sebelum ini.
Katanya, penentangan terhadap Najib dan budaya politik dikaitkan dengan skandal 1MDB adalah asas kepada penubuhan Pejuang, sekali gus membezakannya daripada parti berteraskan Melayu yang lain.

“Jika Pejuang melonggarkan pendirian antirasuahnya semata-mata untuk terus mendapat akses kepada jentera PN, parti itu mungkin dapat bertahan dari segi organisasi tetapi menjadi tidak relevan dari sudut politik kerana pengundi tidak lagi memahami apa yang diperjuangkannya,” katanya kepada FMT.

Asrul mengakui Pejuang yang ditubuhkan bekas perdana menteri Dr Mahathir Mohamad pada 2021, sememangnya sudah lemah dan pengundurannya daripada PN boleh menyebabkan parti itu semakin tidak relevan dalam politik.

Bagaimanapun, katanya PN yang disertai Pejuang kini bukan lagi entiti sama ketika diterajui Presiden Bersatu Muhyiddin Yassin dengan PAS, ketika ini menerajui gabungan itu dan dilihat semakin mesra dengan Najib serta Umno.
Beliau memberi amaran, ketidakjelasan berpanjangan mengenai perkara itu boleh menyebabkan sebahagian kecil pemimpin dan anggota Pejuang yang masih ada menjauhkan diri.

Asrul turut berkata, ruang untuk Pejuang mungkin terhad jika berlaku kerjasama antara PN dan Barisan Nasional (BN), memandangkan sebarang pengaturan pilihan raya dijangka memberi keutamaan kepada Umno, PAS dan Wawasan pimpinan Ketua Pembangkang Hamzah Zainudin.
“Umno mempunyai jenama nasionalis Melayu dan jentera yang kukuh, PAS ada rangkaian akar umbi, manakala Wawasan pimpinan Hamzah membawa wakil rakyat serta rangkaian bekas Bersatu.

“Pejuang berisiko dianggap sebagai rakan pinggiran. Parti itu perlu menentukan sama ada akses kepada jentera pilihan raya PN berbaloi dengan hakisan identitinya dan sama ada pemain utama PN benar-benar memerlukan Pejuang.”

Di bawah pengampunan bersyarat bagi sabitan Najib dalam kes SRC International, beliau dibenarkan menjalani baki hukuman penjara di rumah jika membayar denda RM50 juta, yang sudah dikurangkan daripada jumlah asal RM210 juta.

Umno melancarkan tabung untuk membantu bekas presidennya melunaskan denda itu, manakala PAS berkata pihaknya percaya Najib masih boleh menyumbang kepada negara walaupun menjalani tahanan di rumah. Wawasan pula berkata pihaknya bersyukur keputusan itu menamatkan polemik berhubung pengampunan Najib.

Bagaimanapun, Ketua Penerangan Pejuang, Rafique Rashid Ali, menggesa penjelasan mengenai mekanisme dan syarat bagi banduan diberikan tahanan di rumah, sambil memberi amaran ia tidak hanya dibenarkan kepada golongan elit.

Asrul menyifatkan kenyataan Rafique sebagai 'berhati-hati', secara halus menegaskan pendirian Pejuang mengenai Najib tanpa mempersoalkan kuasa Perlembagaan Yang di-Pertuan Agong untuk memberikan pengampunan atau berdepan secara langsung dengan PAS dan Umno.

“Beliau juga mungkin sedang menguji sejauh mana ruang yang ada untuk Pejuang mengekalkan identiti bebas dalam PN. Namun akhirnya, parti itu perlu menunjukkan sama ada ia akan mempertahankan pendirian tersebut apabila berbuat demikian membawa kesan politik yang sebenar.”
Pragmatik dan kelangsungan lebih penting

Bagaimanapun, Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid dari Universiti Sains Malaysia berkata Pejuang perlu lebih pragmatik dalam perkara itu, sambil menegaskan tahap relevan dan kewujudan jangka panjang parti tersebut menjadi taruhan.

Katanya, kekal bersama PN membolehkan Pejuang memenangi beberapa kerusi Parlimen, malah berkemungkinan mendapat tempat dalam Jemaah Menteri jika gabungan itu berjaya membentuk dan menerajui kerajaan selepas PRU akan datang.
Beliau berkata, semua faktor itu menentukan kelangsungan dan tahap relevan sesebuah parti.
Fauzi berkata, Pejuang boleh memilih untuk mengambil pendirian lebih berprinsip mengenai Najib dan isu rasuah secara umum dalam perbincangan dalaman PN.

“Kehadiran Pejuang dalam PN juga mungkin penting kepada gabungan itu kerana ia menunjukkan demokrasi dalaman PN dengan membenarkan perbezaan pendapat. Tambahan pula, tidak semua dalam PN akan menerima layanan istimewa BN terhadap Najib, walaupun hubungan BN dengan PN semakin rapat.”
Katanya, kenyataan Rafique tidak mungkin menjejaskan hubungan dengan PAS atau Umno kerana Mukhriz Mahathir ialah presiden Pejuang dan tidak menyentuh mengenai pengampunan Najib.
“Selagi Mukhriz berdiam diri mengenai perkara itu, mereka tidak sepatutnya mengesyaki bahawa Pejuang berminat untuk menyimpang daripada pendirian rasmi PN buat masa ini,” katanya.
a4884182516be52b: PETALING JAYA: With 54.4% of Malaysian adults classified as overweight or obese according to the National Health and Morbidity Survey 2023, it is understandable that many are searching for a quick solution.

Cutting carbohydrates may seem like the obvious answer. However, carbohydrates are not uniquely responsible for weight gain, and completely removing them is neither necessary nor practical for most people.

Over time, weight loss requires us to consume less energy than our bodies use, creating what is known as a calorie deficit. This can be achieved in different ways: by reducing portions, eating fewer energy-dense foods, cooking with less fat, cutting back on sugary drinks, or becoming more physically active.
Reducing carbohydrates is one approach, but research comparing low-carb diets with balanced-carb diets has generally found little to no difference in weight loss over one to two years.
The best eating plan is not necessarily the most restrictive. It is one that provides good nutrition, manages hunger, and fits comfortably enough into your life to be sustained.

For Malaysians, banning rice, noodles, bread and other familiar foods can make family meals and social occasions unnecessarily difficult. Feeling deprived may also leave people preoccupied with forbidden foods and more likely to abandon the diet.
Why cutting carb appears to work quickly
Very-low-carb diets can produce an impressive drop on the scales during the first week or two - but not all of it is body fat.
Our bodies store carbohydrates as glycogen in the muscles and liver, along with water. When carb intake falls sharply, glycogen stores decrease and some of this water is released.

Once carbs are reintroduced, glycogen and water stores are replenished, so some of the weight may return. This reflects a normal change in body water and does not mean eating carbohydrates has automatically caused body-fat regain.

Also, carbohydrates are not one uniform group. Complex-carbohydrate foods such as whole grains, oats, beans, dhal, chickpeas, corn and sweet potatoes generally retain more fibre and are often digested more slowly, helping you feel satisfied for longer.

Refined-carbohydrate foods have undergone more processing, which may remove much of their natural fibre. Sugar is also a carbohydrate, and sweetened drinks, desserts, confectionery, pastries and biscuits can provide it in concentrated amounts while offering less fullness than fibre-rich foods.
For weight management, the aim is not to avoid all carbohydrates but to choose fibre-rich, minimally processed sources more often, while limiting foods and drinks high in added sugar.
What to do instead of giving up carbs
1. Keep portions in perspective

Use the Malaysian Healthy Plate as a guide: fill a quarter of your plate with rice, noodles, bread or another carbohydrate, a quarter with protein, and half with vegetables and fruit. Your needs will vary depending on your body size, activity level and overall health.
2. Build a balanced meal
Rice or noodles paired with fish, chicken, eggs, tofu or tempeh and plenty of vegetables will usually be more satisfying than a large serving of carbohydrates with little protein or fibre.
3. Choose higher-fibre options where practical

Brown or mixed-grain rice, wholemeal bread, oats, beans, dhal and sweet potatoes can help boost fibre intake. You don't need to make a direct change overnight; mixing brown rice with white rice, for example, is a good start.
4. Pay attention to drinks

Teh tarik, syrup drinks, bubble tea, soft drinks and other sweetened beverages can add considerable sugar and calories without providing the fullness of a meal. For some people, cutting back on these may help more than eliminating carbs altogether.
5. Be consistent, not extreme
Progress does not require deprivation. A sustainable reduction in portions and energy-dense foods is more valuable than following a strict plan for two weeks and then giving up.
Rice, roti and noodles are not the enemy. How much we eat, what we pair them with and the overall quality of our diet matter far more than whether carbohydrates appear on the plate.

Indra Balaratnam is a consultant dietitian and a fellow of the Malaysian Dietitians’ Association. She runs her own private practice, Indra Balaratnam Nutrition, in Kuala Lumpur. Connect with her on Facebook and Instagram.
aa90d085d621c0a5: PETALING JAYA: Naib Presiden Warisan Junz Wong mencadangkan kerajaan Sabah dan Sarawak mempertimbangkan untuk merangka satu 'manifesto' bersama bagi memperjuangkan kepentingan bersama antara kedua-dua negeri Borneo itu.
Dalam apa yang dilihat sebagai usaha baharu untuk membentuk 'blok Borneo', Wong berkata kedua-dua negeri mempunyai banyak isu yang sama dan perlu bekerjasama rapat.
“Kita perlu bekerjasama 100%. Kita juga sepatutnya mempunyai manifesto rentas sempadan yang membincangkan tentang kedua-dua negeri memperjuangkan perkara yang sama.

“Kita mempunyai banyak perkara sama yang kita perjuangkan, dan juga untuk Malaysia, bukan hanya untuk Sabah dan Sarawak,” kata Adun Tanjung Aru itu pada forum bertajuk 'Unity in Diversity' di Universiti HELP baru-baru ini.

Beliau menjawab soalan daripada seorang lagi ahli panel, Ahli Parlimen Julau Larry Sng, yang bertanya sama ada Wong menjangkakan Sabah akan menerima bahagian yang adil daripada apa yang dipersetujui di bawah Perjanjian Malaysia 1963 (MA63) dalam masa terdekat.
Wong berkata perkara itu bergantung pada perkembangan politik di Malaysia Barat serta keupayaan Sabah untuk bersatu dari segi politik dan bekerjasama dengan Sarawak.

Bekas menteri negeri itu menambah bahawa kerjasama antara kedua-dua negeri di Malaysia Timur harus melangkaui usaha memperjuangkan hak mereka dan merangkumi hala tuju ekonomi bersama untuk tempoh lima tahun akan datang.

Idea mengenai blok Borneo mula timbul pada 2010 sebagai gabungan parti politik apabila Jeffrey Kitingan daripada Parti Solidariti Tanah Airku mengumumkan penubuhan 'Barisan Borneo Bersatu' untuk memperjuangkan hak Sabah dan Sarawak di bawah MA63.
Idea itu timbul semula susulan keluarnya parti-parti pemerintah Sarawak daripada Barisan Nasional pada 2018.
Awal bulan ini, Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim berkata Perlembagaan Persekutuan akan dipinda untuk meningkatkan wakil Sabah dan Sarawak di Parlimen selaras dengan MA63.
Antara isu lain yang masih belum diselesaikan termasuk hak Sabah terhadap 40% hasil bersih dan tuntutan Sarawak berkaitan petroleum.
581f549438b3a042: SANTA MARTA, (Colombia): Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella sent troops into the Caribbean city of Santa Marta on Tuesday after gunmen attacked shops and burnt vehicles following the killing of one of their leaders.

Videos shared online showed members of the self-styled Conquering Self-Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN) riding through the city on motorbikes, firing on businesses that remained open despite the group announcing a 48-hour curfew.
Santa Marta acts as a gateway to Tayrona National Park, a popular tourist destination overlooking the Caribbean.
AFP journalists saw a truck ablaze in the middle of a road and a charred bus on another street.
Dozens of shops were shuttered and parts of the city were deserted.

The chaos followed an earlier announcement by De la Espriella that the police and air force had killed 13 members of the ACSN, an armed group with roots in Colombia's now-defunct paramilitary movement that lives off extortion and cocaine trafficking.
The president said that the 13 "narcoterrorists" killed included the ACSN's second-in-command, who went by the alias "Cholo."
De la Espriella said in a later video statement that he had ordered "that Santa Marta be militarised."

Following the military operation against the ACSN, "these criminals are trying to set a large part of the Caribbean region on fire," he said, adding that "anyone who does not submit will be taken down."
De la Espriella said on X that he had arrived in Santa Marta to oversee the crackdown.
Army troops were deployed along the highway that connects the city with the La Guajira department on the Venezuelan border, where ACSN also operates.

US-backed millionaire De la Espriella pledged a heavy hand against Colombia's myriad drug-running groups — from dissident members of the defunct Marxist rebel army FARC to the former paramilitary groups set up to fight the guerrillas — when he took office in August.
He has ordered bombing raids on guerrilla camps in several parts of the country and held press conferences next to the corpses of rebels laid out in body bags.
"Cholo" is the second senior ACSN member to be killed by the security forces in less than a month, after another commander, "Bendito Menor," was killed in La Guajira.
The ACSN is one of the many armed groups that De la Espriella's leftist predecessor Gustavo Petro had engaged in failed peace talks with.
The Office of the High Commissioner for Peace in Colombia estimates the group has around 800 members.
De la Espriella has ended all dialogue with armed groups and vowed to put them either "in prison or a tomb," with the help of the United States. — AFP
83e94a32e52480e5: UNITED NATIONS: The United States on Wednesday announced the release of an additional US$267 million in funding to support the fight against the ongoing Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

"To date, the United States government has provided US$887 million in direct health and humanitarian assistance to combat the Ebola outbreak," the US state department said in a statement, adding that Washington was the largest aid provider for the latest outbreak.
The aid announcement, made on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, also seeks to "call on capable nations to increase burden sharing to meet the urgency of the moment," the statement said.

Outgoing UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres last month issued an appeal to raise an additional $1.1 billion in aid against the epidemic, which continues to spread to new parts of the DRC, according to the NGO Doctors Without Borders (MSF).
The Ebola outbreak has killed more than 3,600 people and infected 7,500 since mid-May, according to Congolese public health officials, making it the DRC's worst recorded epidemic of the disease.
024e579857a03dc8: RAMALLAH: Israeli ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter said his son was the soldier injured in a car-ramming attack on Wednesday in the occupied West Bank.

Israeli police said earlier a Palestinian man drove a car at high speed towards a policewoman and a soldier who were conducting vehicle searches at an intersection near the Israeli settlement of Beit Horon west of Ramallah.
"As a result, the soldier was wounded and is currently receiving medical treatment. The attacker was killed by the forces," the police added.
Israel's Magen David Adom emergency services said its teams had evacuated a man in serious condition to hospital.
Ambassador Leiter said his son was the injured soldier, adding: "Neria needs a miracle."
"Neria continued to serve in the reserves after losing his older brother, Moshe Yedidya Leiter," he added on X, referring to another son who was killed in action in Gaza in November 2023.
Israeli politicians responded with words of support.
"My wife Sara and I, together with all the people of Israel, are praying for a miracle," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a post on X.
Israel's public broadcaster Kan reported that the ambassador was meant to attend Netanyahu's speech at the UN General Assembly on Thursday, but was instead flying back to Israel to see his son.
Netanyahu's office said the prime minister visited Neria Leiter in the hospital before departing for the United States.
The statement said Leiter was "very seriously wounded" in the attack.

The Palestinian Health Ministry said it had been informed of the death of 29-year-old Mahmoud Mohammad Mahmoud Suleiman, "who was shot by Israeli forces near the village of Beit Ur al-Tahta, west of Ramallah."
It added that Israeli authorities were withholding his body.
Beit Ur al-Tahta mayor Hazem Suleiman, who is not related to Mahmoud Suleiman, told AFP that Israeli forces raided the village and searched the man's family home.
"The town is closed off, with all its entrances blocked. There is no social or commercial activity, and no signs of normal life," he said, adding that the army had also searched other houses.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and violence there has surged since Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel that sparked the Gaza war.
On Sunday, an Israeli settler was shot dead in the West Bank, with the military saying it had arrested the suspected gunman.
That same day, Israel's military also reported an attempted car-ramming in the West Bank, in which the perpetrator was killed.
According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian Health Ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed 1,110 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war.
Israeli figures show at least 49 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.

200f4af6de837f79: LONDON: Bukayo Saka believes the England squad still have a "scar in us" following their agonising World Cup semi-final defeat.

England begin their Nations League campaign against world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday just nine weeks after they conceded two late goals in a painful last-four loss to Lionel Messi's Argentina in Atlanta.
Saka scored a hat-trick as England beat France 6-4 to finish third at the World Cup.
But the 25-year-old Arsenal winger made it clear that the pain of failing to win England's first major men's international football title since a 1966 World Cup triumph on home soil ran deep.
"Obviously, there's still a scar in us," Saka told the BBC on Wednesday. "When you believed, and everyone was so united and so confident we could do it, not just us, but the whole country.
"We're trying to draw a line under it now and focus on the new international season and what we have coming up now.
"You try to move on as soon as possible, but you know, a scar is a scar (and) decides to heal when it heals itself.
"But like I said, we've come here to a new international season, and we've got four massive, difficult group games to try to qualify us in the Nations League, which we're fully focused on."

Saka, managing an Achilles injury throughout the World Cup in North America, remained on the bench during thee semi-final defeat Argentina as England manager Tuchel opted for defensive substitutes in what proved to be an unsuccessful bid to hold on to a 1-0 lead.
Tuchel faced fierce criticism for his tactics as England sat on their advantage against Argentina before his side's late collapse in Atlanta.
"We have had critical reviews that will stay, of course, behind closed doors," said Tuchel when unveiling his Nations League squad last week as he looks to guide England to Euro 2028 glory.
"I am the biggest critic of myself, and reflection is sometimes necessary to get better, and experience is a crucial part of coaching," the 53-year-old German added.
Euro 2028 will be co-hosted by England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland. - AFP
2e4e0efd4c85374e: SYDNEY: Australia said on Wednesday that an AI agent developed by OpenAI breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access to public and non-public files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.
The breach marks one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the US and could fuel concerns about developers' ability to contain the technology.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the medical statistics portal of a government agency responsible for non-sensitive health data and statistics, including public medical spending.

"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the ... network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," Albanese said during a media briefing in New York, where he is attending the UN General Assembly.
He said investigations continue, and Australia has expressed its "extreme concern about this incident" directly to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman.

The incident comes after OpenAI and Anthropic, in separate submissions to a parliamentary inquiry this month, urged Australia to reconsider a ban preventing them from using the country's creative content to train their models.

In a statement, OpenAI said it "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend."
"Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names," it said.
Australian defence minister Richard Marles said that though the hack occurred in June, the government became aware of the incident "a couple of weeks ago".

The breach is one of several recent incidents in which OpenAI has disclosed hacks or unauthorised activity involving its AI agents well after they occurred – in some cases because the activity was only detected belatedly, and in others because the company initially elected not to disclose it.

A separate high-profile incident, a mid-July intrusion into open-source AI repository Hugging Face, was only detected about a week after it took place, according to timelines released by OpenAI and independent investigators. This helped ignite a global conversation about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI models.
Rivals Anthropic, Google's Gemini, and Meta have also disclosed incidents of their agents accessing external systems.
Some of America's top AI executives, including Altman, have called for a slowdown of AI development, citing, among other things, the threat of devastating cyber attacks by out-of-control agents.
6a06cb7d794e7c58: BAKU: Lewis Hamilton on Wednesday said he hopes that this year's Formula One world championship will conclude with its two races as scheduled in the Middle East despite the continuing conflict.

"From what I have read, things seem ok out there, but I don't have all the information and I don't know what the risk levels are.

"And we have a lot of races where it's only a one-stop. It's not particularly challenging.

The 41-year-old veteran of 394 grands prix said he felt the sport should make greater demands of the drivers, not fewer.

Compatriots George Russell of Mercedes and world champion Lando Norris of McLaren were less concerned.

"We need to make our sport better and rely more on driving, rather than who can look after their battery the best," he added. - AFP

ab684995edb46cbb: SHENZHEN Cristina Bucsa overcame fatigue and rebounded from a disappointing singles loss to help Spain punch their ticket to the Billie Jean King Cup semi-finals for the first time since 2008 in Shenzhen on Wednesday.

Bucsa and her teammate Sara Sorribes Tormo secured the deciding doubles point by triumphing 6-2, 7-5 over Anna Danilina and Zhibek Kulambayeva to clinch the quarter-final tie for Spain over Kazakhstan.
The Spanish pair saved a whopping 18 out of 20 break points throughout the gruelling two-hour seven-minute doubles affair. The second set alone lasted 88 minutes.

"The girls, they have really good fighting spirit, they put in all their heart and passion. I'm really proud of all of them. But the competition doesn't end here, we have semi-finals on Friday," said Spain's team captain Carla Suarez Navarro.

Spain's Jessica Bouzas Maneiro claimed the opening point of the tie with a 6-2, 6-2 win over Sonja Zhiyenbayeva, before world number 79 Yulia Putintseva kept Kazakhstan alive in the contest by defeating Bucsa 6-2, 3-6, 6-1.
Putintseva's victory, her 28th in the competition, saw her equal the record held by Galina Voskoboeva for most BJK Cup matches won by a Kazakh player.
Bucsa had arrived late in Shenzhen after reaching the singles semi-finals and winning the doubles title at the WTA tournament in Guadalajara last weekend.
The long trek from Mexico to China may have accounted for her slow start against Putintseva, who played a near-flawless opening set to take the lead in just 33 minutes.
Bucsa dug deep in the second, countering Putintseva's drop shots with her own mix of big-hitting and soft touches to level the match.
But the 35th-ranked Spaniard ran out of gas in the third, as Putintseva swung the momentum back in her favour to clinch the win and take the quarter-final tie into a deciding doubles showdown.
Double duty for Bucsa
The day was not over for Bucsa, who was back on court some 30 minutes later to partner up with Sorribes Tormo in doubles.

As the highest-ranked Spanish player in both singles and doubles, the Moldova-born Bucsa knew her team were relying on her to pull off double duty in Shenzhen and the 28-year-old did not disappoint, as she sealed the deal alongside Sorribes Tormo to send Spain through to a semi-final meeting with the Czech Republic.
Earlier in the day, Bouzas Maneiro got the Spaniards off to a flying start, easing past Zhiyenbayeva in a mere 62 minutes.
The Spanish world number 93 faced zero break points, broke her opponent four times and won 82 per cent of the points behind her first serve to give her team a 1-0 lead against Kazakhstan.

Zhiyenbayeva, a 20-year-old ranked 384 in the world, was playing just her second-ever match in the BJK Cup, having made her competition debut during Kazakhstan's victory against Canada in the qualifiers earlier this year.
"For me it was a very short match, unfortunately. I wish I could have done better," said a disappointed Zhiyenbayeva.
The action continues on Thursday with the two remaining quarter-finals taking place at the Shenzhen Bay Sports Centre.

90c5915417d99831: FRANKFURT: Germany on Wednesday unveiled a roadmap for abandoning fossil fuels by 2045, making Europe's largest economy only the third country to have done so after France and the Netherlands.
Though almost 200 countries pledged at COP28 climate negotiations in 2023 to wean off fossil fuels, few have presented concrete plans, Germany's environment ministry said.

German environment minister Carsten Schneider told the UN General Assembly that the Middle East war showed why fossil fuels should be dumped.
"It is not just extreme weather events around the world that demonstrate how urgently we need to do more to protect the climate," he said.
"If the situation in the Strait of Hormuz determines whether people can still afford their daily commute to work, that is not a good state of affairs," he added.
Fentje Jacobsen, a climate policy advisor at the WWF, said the roadmap largely restated existing iniatives without adding "new ideas or additional ambitions".

Energy minister Katherina Reiche favours building new gas-fired power plants to help stabilise the electricity grid and help offset the intermittency of renewable sources like wind and solar.

KUALA LUMPUR: An electoral understanding under the Pakatan Harapan Plus framework may be the most practical path forward for Bersatu following its split with Pas.
Universiti Malaya political analyst Dr Mohammad Tawfik Yaakub said Bersatu was likely to explore new electoral arrangements as going solo would be a high-risk option.
He said making a new pact was a priority to avoid isolation and prevent multi-cornered contests from eroding its support.
"A PH Plus arrangement may be the most practical avenue if formal cooperation with Pas is no longer possible," he said.
"However, this depends on whether both sides can agree on a limited, seat-by-seat understanding rather than a full political alliance."
On Saturday, Melaka PH said it was finalising negotiations with parties that shared similar aspirations, including Bersatu, to form a PH Plus collaboration to contest the Melaka election.
Melaka PH chairman Adly Zahari said the negotiations were being conducted based on decisions made at a PH presidential council meeting.
"The negotiations also included Bersatu, but any form of cooperation will only be announced after the negotiation process has been completed," he said.
Tawfik said cooperation with Barisan Nasional remained unlikely given their direct competition for Malay support and unresolved political differences.

"Retaining its (single) seat will be difficult if Bersatu faces Pas, BN and PH separately. Its advantage will depend heavily on the strength of local candidates, incumbency, grassroots machinery, and whether Malay votes are fragmented among several blocs."
As for other seats, he said that would only be realistic if Bersatu secured an electoral pact or a strategic understanding that prevented three- or four-cornered fights.
"Without such mechanisms, the contest will descend into a battle of machinery, local credibility and vote consolidation."
While contesting under its own logo remains an option, Tawfik said Bersatu carried significant electoral risk.
"Bersatu may, therefore, prefer a selective electoral pact, potentially under the PH Plus framework, to protect strategic seats and reduce vote-splitting.
"The main issue is whether such an arrangement can be accepted by PH supporters and Bersatu's grassroots without causing backlash or weakening campaign mobilisation."

Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities Associate Professor Dr Mazlan Ali said PH Plus could be an ideal choice because, apart from PH, no political party or coalition was equal in strength to BN and Pas.
"I believe Bersatu will establish ties with other coalitions to boost its strength and chances of winning, because contesting solo would split votes.
"PH is the best option for Bersatu in the Melaka election."
He added that Bersatu had a 50-50 chance of retaining the Sungai Udang seat and winning back Bemban but with PH, it would stand a better chance.
Bersatu won both seats in the previous election, but its Bemban assemblyman was later expelled from the party.
"I do not expect Bersatu to win more seats unless it is a fight involving BN, Pas and PH."
Melaka will hold its 16th election soon following the dissolution of the state assembly yesterday.
The Melaka assembly has 28 seats, with BN having won 21 in the previous election.

5a072d88f84f002c: NANNING, Sept 24 — China opened the Pinglu Canal recently, giving its landlocked south-west a shortcut to the coast and overseas markets, particularly those in the Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean), the country’s largest trading partner.

Built at a cost of 72.7 billion yuan (about RM43.8 billion), the 134.2-kilometer canal runs from Hengzhou, a county-level city in south China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, to the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of south-west China.
The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China’s inland regions with Asean and other global markets.
It is the first river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949.

Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal shortens the inland waterway journey for goods from south-west China to the sea by more than 560 kilometers compared with traditional routes through ports in Guangdong Province.
It is expected to reduce overall logistics costs by 18 to 30 per cent and save more than 5 billion yuan in transportation costs each year.
Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government of Guangxi, said the canal creates a new link between China’s market of 1.4 billion people and Asean’s nearly 700 million consumers.
Its impact, Lu said, could extend beyond the movement of goods, spurring new cross-border investment and deepening regional supply-chain integration.

The canal took over four years to build. Most of it was created by widening, deepening and straightening existing waterways, while a small section had to be excavated through dry land and mountainous terrain.
“There was no established model or ready-made precedent to follow,” said Cheng Yaofei, chairman of Guangxi Pinglu Canal Construction Co, Ltd.

A drone photo taken on June 8, 2026 shows a view of the dedicated wildlife corridor bridge of the Pinglu Canal in Jiuzhou Town, Lingshan County of Qinzhou City in south China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. — Xinhua pic via The Borneo Post
One of the biggest engineering challenges was a 65-meter difference in water level, roughly the height of a 20-plus-story building.
Three navigation hubs, all featuring twin-line ship locks, were built to raise and lower vessels along the canal.
Engineers developed water-recycling systems at the hubs, enabling the canal to save more than 1 billion cubic meters of water annually.
Environmental protection was another priority during construction.

More than 98 per cent of the roughly 315 million cubic meters of earth and rock excavated during construction was reused. The canal also includes a fish passage more than 480 meters long and a dedicated wildlife crossing for land animals including leopard cats and squirrels.

The canal opens in the first year of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), as the world’s second-largest economy seeks to promote more coordinated regional development and further expand high-standard opening up — priorities outlined in the plan.
The new artery carries particular significance for China’s south-west, which has long lagged behind the more prosperous eastern coast and faced higher costs getting goods to seaports.
Coal, ore, grain, new-energy materials and auto parts from the region can now take a more direct route to overseas markets.

In the near term, the canal is likely to reshape existing cargo flows, with some freight shifting from road and rail to waterways and from the Pearl River Estuary to the Beibu Gulf, said Meng Shuang, an associate professor at Central University of Finance and Economics.
Over time, Meng said, the lower cost of reaching the sea could generate new trade, draw investment inland and reshape industrial development along the canal.

With China and Asean seeking closer economic ties and greater regional connectivity, experts say the Pinglu Canal could provide a new corridor for goods to flow in both directions between the vast Chinese and Asean markets.

China’s trade with Asean exceeded US$1 trillion for the first time last year. In the first seven months of 2026, total trade between the two sides reached US$744.41 billion, an increase of 24.7 per cent year on year, accounting for 21.8 per cent of China’s total foreign trade during this period.
BeBe Zhao, president of Singapore-China Integrated Developments (Guangxi) Pte Ltd, said the canal could bring new opportunities for businesses on both sides.
Asean products could move more efficiently into western China, while goods manufactured there could reach global markets through regional hubs such as Singapore.
“The new route will not only make trade more efficient but also strengthen Singapore’s role as a regional transshipment and trade hub,” Zhao said.
For Boonsub Panichakarn from the Faculty of Logistics and Digital Supply Chain at Naresuan University in Thailand, the canal’s significance goes beyond the distance it saves.
It lies in how much the canal can reduce logistics costs, time variability and uncertainty across the entire Asean-south-west China supply chain, he said. — Xinhua via The Borneo Post
7063d6fa15dd8b05: BANGKOK, Sept 24 — From a working-class childhood on the southern English coast to the top foreign-born monk in Thailand, Shaun Chiverton’s quest for a better life has taken him further than most.

Five decades after he travelled to India to follow the Buddha’s teachings, the 68-year-old this summer became the first non-Thai to be elevated to the rank of Somdet Phra Rachakhana, or royal monastic leader — the second-highest level in Thailand’s monkhood.
“My father said, ‘Well, we always knew he’d do something weird, we just didn’t know what kind of weird it would be’,” the monk, now known as Ajahn (Teacher) Jayasaro, told AFP with a smile.
But he understood: “My dad said, ‘Look, I just want you to be happy’.”
He grew up in a secular family on the Isle of Wight, a bookish child in a small town who from his teens was driven by some big questions.
“One was, what’s the best way to live your life as a human being?” Jayasaro said in a recent interview at a retreat centre near Bangkok.
“And second, given that there’s so much suffering and injustice and violence in the world, could the world be better than it is?”
Jayasaro became interested in Buddhism and set off for India, travelling around the region before settling in Thailand, where he became a monk.
After previously feeling like “a kind of freak”, he said he arrived at a monastery in northeast Thailand to find “everybody more or less shares the same views and aspirations — it’s just wonderful”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

British and Thai Buddhist monk Shaun Chiverton, now known as Ajahn Jayasaro, speaks with devotees in Bangkok on September 1, 2026. From a working-class childhood on the southern English coast to the top foreign-born monk in Thailand, Chiverton's quest for a better life has taken him further than most. Five decades after he travelled to India to follow the Buddha's teachings, the 68-year-old this summer became the first non-Thai to be elevated to rank of Somdet Phra Rachakhana, or royal monastic leader -- the second-highest level in Thailand's monkhood. — AFP pic
‘Completely unqualified’

Jayasaro joined the forest monks of Theravada Buddhism, who lead an austere life of discipline, renunciation and meditation, and has spent much of the past two decades in a hermitage near the Khao Yai mountains.
He has written several books in English and Thai, and holds regular retreats. His YouTube channel has 100,000 subscribers.
He was granted Thai citizenship by royal decree in 2020 and has received numerous royal promotions, culminating in his latest elevation which made him one of just 18 at that rank.
“In many ways I’m completely unqualified,” he said, comparing his “completely left-field” forest life to other senior monks who lead top monasteries.
But his background gives him particular insight, he noted.
“I have a broader knowledge in terms of relating traditional Buddhist teachings to the changing world that we live in,” he said.
He supports the broad ban on female ordinations in Thai Buddhism, but said there should be a way to accommodate women who wanted to study and practice.
“There are women with a genuine spiritual vocation and we need to be able to provide a vehicle and a way for them to live a life,” he said.
Jayasaro’s teachings emphasise the importance of living a good life and letting go of material things and negative habits to develop more “noble” qualities, such as kindness and compassion.
Not all Buddhists adhere to this, and Jayasaro acknowledged “a certain amount of corruption” even within the monkhood, after a series of sex and fraud scandals.
Old age and death
The Buddha lived around 2,500 years ago, but Jayasaro said his teachings offer “timeless” tools to manage the challenges of modern life.
“People are really stressed out these days. There’s an epidemic of depression and anxiety. But these are not new mental states… and there are ways of dealing with them,” he said.
He lamented the rise of “almost manic individualism”, which he linked to mental health issues, particularly among young people.
“Saying that ‘you can be whatever you want to be’ is just really unfair on children,” he said.
“A lot of people wake up when they’re in their 30s or 40s and realise, no, they’re not going to be what they want to be.
“And then where do you go from there?”
The same question can be asked of Jayasaro.
“The classic Buddhist answer would be old age, sickness and death, I think, a very blunt answer,” he said with a laugh.
In fact, his next step is writing a TV series in English for YouTube, focused on an “everyman” figure in the time of the Buddha.
He hopes it will help others benefit from the teachings that have shaped him.
“I just feel an incredibly fortunate human being to have been able to live the life I have,” he said. “I just have a happy life.” — AFP

f4f54d599708f4cc: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 24 — With Malaysia bracing for an intensification of El Niño conditions, prolonged extreme heat could affect the country’s poultry production, particularly if high temperatures persist for days or weeks.
The effects could include slower growth in broiler chickens, higher mortality and lower egg production, potentially putting pressure on Malaysia’s chicken and egg supply.
However, experts and poultry farmers caution that extreme heat will not automatically lead to a national shortage.

Professor Datuk Zulkifli Idrus, director of the Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Food Security at Universiti Putra Malaysia, said the severity and duration of the heat, as well as how well farms are prepared, would determine the impact on production.
“A short heatwave is not likely to seriously disrupt national supply.
“It’s the prolonged, widespread extreme heat that worries people, but how much depends on farm preparedness.
“A Super El Niño wouldn’t necessarily lead to a national chicken or egg shortage,” he said.
How could heat affect chicken production?
Broiler chickens consume less feed during hot weather because digestion and metabolism generate additional body heat.
As a result, heat-stressed birds can grow more slowly and become less efficient at converting feed into body weight.
“Heat stress also increases the release of stress hormones, particularly corticosterone, which can alter metabolism, reduce growth, harm gut health and impair feed efficiency,” Zulkifli said.
Modern broilers are particularly vulnerable because they grow rapidly and generate considerable body heat.
Heavier birds nearing market weight can have greater difficulty shedding excess heat, making them more susceptible during prolonged periods of high temperatures.
Severe or prolonged heat stress can also increase mortality.
Zulkifli said deaths could occur within hours during a severe heat event, particularly among heavier birds, if the chickens are unable to dissipate enough body heat.
However, he said there was no single estimate for how much mortality could increase across Malaysia because losses would vary between farms.
Factors such as housing, ventilation, cooling, stocking density, bird age, water supply and farm management would all influence the outcome.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Large exhaust fans inside Mohd Muzamri Shoib’s closed-house chicken farm. — Picture by Yusof Isa
What about egg production?
Laying hens can also experience reduced productivity during prolonged heat.
When temperatures rise, hens eat less, reducing the nutrients and energy available for egg production.
Prolonged heat exposure can also increase stress hormone levels and interfere with reproductive processes and egg development.
This can result in fewer and smaller eggs, as well as poorer eggshell quality.
“Laying hens can lose egg production quickly as they reduce their feed intake,” Zulkifli said.
While laying hens are generally more heat tolerant than heavier broilers, prolonged heat can still have a significant effect on their productivity.
Could this affect Malaysia’s chicken supply?
Potentially, but the impact would not be immediate.
For broilers, slower growth could mean birds take longer to reach market weight, while higher mortality could reduce the number available for sale.
For eggs, lower production could reduce the quantity entering the market.
If these effects occur across a large number of farms at the same time, overall supply could come under pressure.

Zulkifli said prolonged and widespread extreme heat could therefore affect supply, but the extent would depend on how severe the conditions are and how effectively farmers can mitigate the heat stress.
Mohd Muzamri Shoib, a broiler farmer and chairman of the Selangor Poultry Farmers Association, likewise cautioned against directly linking hot weather to a chicken shortage.
“I would be cautious about saying that hot weather causes a shortage of broiler chickens.

“It would be more accurate to say that excessive and prolonged heat stress can affect broiler production performance, particularly if temperature, drinking water, nutrition and ventilation cannot be properly managed,” he said.
For Muzamri, the key issue is therefore not simply how hot temperatures become, but whether farms can maintain conditions that allow chickens to continue growing normally.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Muzamri inside his closed-house chicken farm in Jalan Kebun, Shah Alam. — Picture by Yusof Isa
Why farm preparedness matters
Zulkifli said farms with better environmental controls should be better equipped to withstand prolonged heat.
Closed-house systems with environmental controls provide greater control over ventilation, temperature and cooling, although they are more expensive to build and operate.
Backup generators are also important, particularly for closed-house farms, where a power failure could stop ventilation and cooling systems.

Nutritional strategies such as probiotics, prebiotics and some phytogenic feed additives may also help chickens cope with heat stress, although these should complement rather than replace proper cooling, ventilation and water supply.
Muzamri said farmers should begin preparing before their chickens show signs of heat stress.
“If El Niño conditions result in a prolonged period of hot weather, in my view, farmers need to make preparations early rather than waiting until the chickens begin showing signs of heat stress.
“Fans, cooling pads, water pumps, sensors, generators and water supplies need to be inspected and maintained more frequently,” he said.
He said his farm also incurs additional costs to purchase ice to help cool the poultry houses during the hottest part of the day, between 11am and 3pm.
So, should consumers expect a chicken shortage?
Not necessarily.
A short heatwave is unlikely to seriously disrupt Malaysia’s national chicken and egg supply.
The bigger concern is a prolonged and widespread period of extreme heat that affects production across multiple farms.
Even then, the extent of any impact on supply would depend on the severity and duration of the heat and how well poultry farmers are able to manage the conditions.
In short, Super El Niño does not automatically mean a chicken shortage, but prolonged heat stress could put pressure on poultry production if farms are unable to keep losses under control.
d8297d9deec6c818: WUHAN, Sept 24 — Across a patchwork of village ponds in central China, rows of floating cages ripple on the water.
Beneath the surface, slender, snake-like rice eels twist through the nets — the fish are a common dish at Chinese meals and a big part of how local farmers make a living.
Also known as the Asian swamp eel, the slippery freshwater fish is still somewhat of a niche delicacy outside of Asia.
In China, however, it is widely consumed and has long been prized for its distinctive flavour and nutritional value.
The ponds are in Xiantao, a major hub for rice eel breeding and farming in Hubei Province.
The city now accounts for roughly one-quarter of China’s rice eel output, according to local industry figures.
The industry began to take shape more than three decades ago, when local farmers started experimenting with raising rice eels in cages.

Getting rice eel farming off the ground wasn’t always easy. When people saw how profitable it could be, producers all over China jumped in, creating an oversupply and sending prices tumbling. A lot of farming communities gave up, but Xiantao stuck with it.

“With much of our farmland converted into ponds, rice eel farming had become the only viable way forward,” said Zhu Chuanbao, Party secretary of Xianfeng Village in Zhanggou Town and president of the Xiantao rice eel industry association.
The village alone produces about one billion rice eels a year.
“That is enough to put Xianfeng’s rice eels on the table of nearly every household in China on average,” Zhu said.
The industry has helped lift villagers out of poverty and onto a path toward prosperity.
Xiantao is now home to China’s biggest rice eel processing enterprise and the largest rice eel trading market at the production site.
The city’s rice eel industry generates an annual output value of over 12 billion yuan (US$1.77 billion or RM7.2 billion).
The growth of this industry has been supported by the central government’s policies to advance rural revitalisation.
China aims to basically achieve modernisation by 2035, and that cannot happen without the modernisation of agriculture and rural areas.
“We are entering a new era of rice eel farming,” said Zhu.

Researchers at Huazhong Agricultural University in Wuhan, the provincial capital, and the Institute of Hydrobiology under the Chinese Academy of Sciences have worked with local producers to develop large-scale artificial breeding techniques and controlled-environment aquaculture systems.
These advances have reduced the industry’s dependence on seasonal cycles, making year-round production possible.
By allowing precise control of water quality and temperature, the systems help farmers cope with increasingly frequent extreme weather.
They also protect rice eels from predators, raising juvenile survival rates in the lab from 50 per cent to 90 per cent.
The real challenge isn’t just raising more rice eels. It’s about getting more people to try them, especially outside Asia where many folks are not as familiar with the fish.

That means tapping overseas markets. In the first half of this year, Xiantao exported more than 125 tonnes of frozen rice eels and processed rice eel products to more than 10 countries and regions, including North America, Australia, Japan, the Republic of Korea and South-east Asia.
“There are more than 60 million overseas Chinese, and rice eels are already widely accepted in East Asia and South-east Asia.
“We are now seeking to reach more consumers in Europe and North America by developing products suited to their tastes, including grilled rice eel and rice eel steaks,” Zhu said.
Rice eel farmers in Xiantao have built a digital platform covering the entire supply chain, from breeding and farming to feeding and processing.
Consumers can use it to trace products through every stage of production.
“Traceability gives Xiantao rice eels the confidence to reach consumers across China and around the world,” said Lu Huawei, a local government official.
Some farmers are already looking ahead to the next technological upgrade.
Xiao Tiebing is closely following the development of an unmanned boat by a local company in collaboration with leading Chinese universities.
Designed to automate repetitive tasks, the vessel can feed the fish and remove uneaten feed.
“I hope new technologies can further improve farming efficiency, just as earlier innovations have done, and help us earn more,” Xiao said. — Xinhua via The Borneo Post
741169360f4d4712: CHOYR (Mongolia), Sept 24 — Peter Catterall and Eenee Purevdorj When Mongolian herder Ganchimeg’s sheep strayed dangerously near a salty lake this summer, driven by hunger as nearby vegetation was poor, she was in a “total panic”.
“If they drank or stepped into it, the whole flock would be destroyed,” she told AFP outside her traditional ger, the tent’s shape silhouetted on the vast horizon of the Gobi Desert.
But thanks to an app helping herders navigate the risks that climate change is bringing to Mongolia, her husband was able to reach the sheep before they drank the brackish water.
“He immediately rushed over at top speed and intercepted them,” said Ganchimeg, a mother of four who, like many Mongolians, goes by just one name.
“If we hadn’t used that GPS tracker, we might have lost our entire flock.”

Herders are on the frontline of both climate change and desertification impacts — climate change is bringing extreme weather, including deadly cold snaps and droughts, which compound desertification caused by overgrazing.
Huge and sparsely populated, Mongolia is disproportionately affected by human-driven climate change, threatening the country’s nomadic population and livestock.

Bilgudei Gankhulug, the 26-year-old founder of the Hunu app used by Ganchimeg, told AFP he was inspired to help herders after a 2024 “dzud” — an extreme weather event that brought temperatures as low as minus 45C.
“Over eight million livestock died. I saw a lot of herders losing their income, losing their livelihoods in just the span of a few months,” said Bilgudei.
Meaning “strong nomad”, the name Hunu “embodies our mission of empowering nomadic herders with the help of technology,” he said.
‘Strong nomad’
The app allows nomads to track their livestock with a solar-charging GPS device attached to one animal per group — sufficient for herds that tend to stick together on the spacious steppe.

It has an artificial intelligence-powered weather feature with updates on the deadly dust storms and blizzards made more common in recent years by climate change, which scientists say is intensifying globally.
The app also compiles useful information on maps showing snow depth, wind direction, soil moisture and drought, assisting nomads in crucial decisions on where to move next.
Mongolia hosted talks on a global desertification treaty, known as COP17, last month.
Countries agreed financing for land restoration and tackling drought resilience, but concerns remain over a massive funding shortfall to the growing problem.
Bilgudei told AFP he hopes to expand Hunu to central Asian countries, and met with pastoralists from Tanzania and Uruguay at COP17 interested too.
“Our problems are pretty similar,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This photo taken on August 25, 2026 shows goats belonging to sheep herder Ganchimeg with painted horns in Bayantal, Mongolia's Govisumber province. Mongolia is disproportionately affected by human-driven climate change, which scientists say is intensifying globally, threatening the country's nomadic population and their livestock. — AFP pic
Global dilemma

About 80 per cent of Mongolia is rangelands, large tracts of unfarmed land covered by native grasses and shrubs, according to Chimeddorj Buyanaa, Mongolia conservation director at the World Wildlife Fund.
“Rangelands are critically important for the local communities and also for the livelihoods of all of the Mongolian people,” he told AFP.
Compounding the issue of climate change is rampant overgrazing that also endangers the region’s wildlife, including snow leopards and saiga antelope, Chimeddorj said.
Around one in four Mongolians are nomadic herders.
Nearly 82 per cent of the country’s territory is affected by desertification and land degradation, authorities said in August.
Many herder families have simply decided to pack up and seek new lives in the city.
“Dundgovi Province’s population has been declining continuously in recent years,” the southern region’s governor, Munkhchuluun Samdannyam, told AFP at COP17.
The worsening climate is a major problem for the province — three-fifths of its economy depends on livestock husbandry, Munkhchuluun said — but consequences are felt further afield.
“Dust storms can begin here and travel south to China, Korea, Japan and even as far as the United States,” Munkhchuluun said.
“(It) is not only Mongolia’s problem.
“It is also a global problem.”
‘Learn from traditions’
Speaking to AFP before heading to milk several camels tethered nearby, 49-year-old herder Bolormaa Erdenee said she was sceptical of forums like COP17.
“I often question whether the true voice of our herders is actually reaching decision-makers or not,” she said.
Bolormaa and her husband raise about 400 livestock.
In their usual summer grazing area, she said roads for heavy mining trucks now criss-cross the steppe, kicking up dust and disrupting her animals.
Several nomadic households nearby have already relocated nearly 200 kilometres (125 miles) away in search of greener pastures.
Hunu app founder Bilgudei — whose ancestors were nomadic herders — said traditional migration itself is a form of environmental protection.
Bilgudei told AFP it’s important to “learn from the traditions… and combine it with the science and technology”. — AFP
1c14b2fb78eb29f0: When President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping meet in Washington today, attention will inevitably focus on trade, tariffs, strategic rivalry and the wider trajectory of Sino-American relations.
Yet another issue may prove even more consequential: artificial intelligence.
International relations are increasingly about how the United States and China manage AI — not merely how they compete over it.

Ahead of the summit, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said Washington had proposed an AI safety notification mechanism through which the two countries could alert each other to AI-related incidents serious enough to affect national security.
The proposal is still preliminary. Its thresholds, procedures and institutional arrangements remain to be negotiated.
Nevertheless, the fact that Washington and Beijing are discussing such a mechanism is important.
Malaysia and Asean must watch carefully.

For decades, international relations have revolved around military power, nuclear deterrence, trade, energy security and strategic waterways. All remain crucial. But AI is rapidly becoming another organising principle of international power.
The states controlling advanced AI models, semiconductor supply chains, computing infrastructure, data and technological talent will possess advantages extending far beyond the digital economy.
AI increasingly touches intelligence, cybersecurity, manufacturing, financial markets, logistics, military planning and critical infrastructure.
The US-China relationship therefore contains two seemingly contradictory dynamics — competition and cooperation.
Competition is unavoidable.
Washington does not want China to overtake the United States in frontier AI. Beijing has equally little intention of accepting permanent technological dependence on America.
Their rivalry consequently extends across semiconductors, computing power, algorithms, data centres, investment and scientific talent.
But cooperation is becoming equally necessary.
Neither country benefits if advanced AI produces catastrophic cyber incidents, disrupts critical infrastructure or generates an escalation that neither government intended.

During the Cold War, Washington and Moscow eventually understood that intense nuclear competition required communication precisely because they distrusted each other. AI increasingly requires a comparable logic.
An AI-related incident affecting electricity grids, financial systems, communications networks or military infrastructure could easily be interpreted as deliberate aggression.
Was an attack authorised? Was it accidental?
Did an autonomous system behave beyond the intentions of its operators? That is potentially a dangerous self recursive improvement system.
Without communication, technological accidents can become geopolitical crises.
This is where Asean has a direct interest.
Southeast Asia sits economically and strategically between the world’s two largest powers.
Asean economies are deeply connected to Chinese manufacturing and trade while simultaneously depending extensively on American technology, investment and financial markets.
Asean cannot afford an AI world divided completely into hostile technological blocs.
Neither should Asean simply accept rules written in Washington and Beijing.
Malaysia and other Asean members must strengthen their capabilities in AI governance, cybersecurity, data protection and technological diplomacy.
Malaysia has particular reasons to pay attention.
Its expanding semiconductor, data centre and AI ecosystems mean that technological sovereignty will increasingly overlap with economic and national security.
But sovereignty does not mean isolation.
No Southeast Asian country can independently control every layer of the AI ecosystem.
Hardware may originate in one country, cloud infrastructure in another, algorithms elsewhere and data across multiple jurisdictions.
Asean must therefore remain polytropous — spreading and deepening its technological relationships without surrendering strategic autonomy to either major power.
Asean’s diplomatic tradition may also have something useful to contribute. Its emphasis on dialogue, confidence-building and incremental institutionalisation can appear slow.
Yet AI governance requires precisely the ability to keep competing powers talking without demanding complete strategic alignment.
The Trump-Xi summit should therefore be watched as more than another encounter between two great powers.

If Washington and Beijing can construct even rudimentary guardrails around dangerous AI incidents, they will have acknowledged an important reality — technological superiority does not eliminate mutual vulnerability.
Malaysia and Asean should support such dialogue while insisting that global AI governance cannot eventually become an exclusive US-China condominium.
Southeast Asia and the wider Global South must have a voice too.
Today, Sept 24, 2026, could therefore mark an important moment in international relations.
The central question of the AI age is no longer simply whether America or China will lead.

It is whether both can compete intensely while establishing sufficient guardrails to prevent their competition — or their increasingly powerful machines — from producing consequences that neither can control.
For Malaysia and Asean, watching this relationship carefully is no longer optional.
It is becoming an essential part of diplomacy in the age of artificial intelligence. Three concrete actions should follow.
First, Malaysia and Asean should establish a regional AI safety and incident-reporting mechanism.

It should connect national regulators, cybersecurity agencies, critical-infrastructure operators and defence establishments, with clear procedures for reporting serious AI failures, which invariably include cyber incidents and unintended system behaviour.
Regular exercises and confidential communication channels would help distinguish accidents from deliberate attacks before they escalate.
Second, Asean should create a permanent regional forum on AI governance and strategic stability.

Meeting regularly under an Asean-led framework, it should bring together governments, technical experts, industry and civil society to develop common standards on testing, transparency, data protection, autonomous systems and the use of AI in security operations.
Asean should also coordinate its positions in global institutions so that Southeast Asia is a rule-maker rather than merely a rule-taker.
Third, Malaysia and its Asean partners should invest collectively in technological autonomy.
This means expanding regional research and development, semiconductor packaging and testing.
Indeed, that includes securing cloud infrastructure, public-interest datasets, AI education and trusted digital infrastructure.
Diversifying suppliers is essential, but so is building indigenous capabilities that reduce dependence on any single external power while preserving openness to international cooperation.
These steps would not make Asean immune to great-power rivalry.
They would, however, give the region greater resilience, bargaining power and strategic choice.
For Malaysia and Asean, watching this relationship carefully is no longer optional.
It is becoming an essential part of diplomacy in the age of artificial intelligence.

0e532aff95f51550: PETALING JAYA: For many, LinkedIn is simply a platform for job hunting or checking what former classmates are up to. For Ayu Shahirah Salem, one post in 2020 changed her career, drawing almost two million impressions and 10,000 likes in 24 hours.

Today, she works as a product designer at global energy corporation BP while pursuing a PhD in information technology. The 29-year-old Sarawakian stands out with more than 125,000 followers and has even appeared on LinkedIn’s Top 50 Malaysia lists.
Originally from Miri, Ayu said it had always been her ambition to work in the industry.

“For most typical Asian families, you’re expected to become a doctor, lawyer or engineer. But in Miri - where oil was first discovered in Malaysia - there’s another requirement: you’re expected to work in oil and gas,” she said with a laugh.

She went on to study software engineering at Universiti Teknologi Petronas, where she excelled academically, winning several competitions and receiving the Chancellor’s Gold Award - the university's highest academic honour.
Then the pandemic disrupted the job market.
Upon the advice of a lecturer, Ayu decided to post her resume on LinkedIn, even though she barely used the platform.
"I was lucky because I'd managed to get a job before I graduated. But I think everyone was struggling to find jobs back then, so I thought, maybe I need to give something back to society."

Much to her surprise, her resume quickly went viral on the platform. This was partly because of its simplicity: at a time when elaborate Canva templates and graphics were popular, she'd decided to focus on content.
Ayu had also researched how resumes were screened by applicant tracking systems before reaching recruiters, and listed what applicants should include to improve their chances of getting noticed.
“Suddenly, people were messaging me saying, ‘Thank you so much, Ayu, for sharing your resume. I've been trying to get a job for one year. I copied your resume format and suddenly I got a job.'"
What began as a single post gradually turned into a much bigger commitment, leading Ayu to challenge herself to post daily for the next two years.

People began asking her to review their resumes, while her content expanded to include interview advice, job-hunting tips and technology resources, alongside career lessons, failures and things she wished she had known as a student.
Soon, those conversations moved beyond the platform, with Ayu invited to speak at talks both online and in person.
One message in particular, which Ayu received after an online talk from a woman who had secured a job shortly after her mother had passed away, stays with her.
“She told me that because she got the job, she felt relieved because at least she could cover the basic costs for her family," Ayu recalled.
"It made me realise that there really was no reason for me to keep what I know to myself."

Her growing audience also created opportunities she could not have anticipated. Ayu was one of 15 delegates, and the only Malaysian, chosen out of 300 global applicants to represent BP at the One Young World youth leadership summit in 2022.

In 2025, she was a regional finalist for the Best Ally Award at the Women in Tech Apac Awards in Kyoto, Japan. And this year, Ayu prominently featured in BP’s billboard campaign at KL Sentral - making her the first Sarawakian woman to become a face of the corporation in Malaysia.

Still, her journey has not been without criticism. “During my first year of posting on LinkedIn, I got a lot of hate. People would send me messages saying, ‘Who are you to talk about careers? You are just a fresh grad. You don’t really have experience.’”
Some even questioned her because of her gender, telling her she was “just a girl”. Today, she is balancing her career with further studies while preparing to write a book.

Perhaps fittingly, her advice to young people now comes with a storyteller’s perspective. “If you’re struggling in life, remember that every main character goes through plot twists and hardships before they reach their happy ending," she said.
Follow Ayu Shahirah Salem on LinkedIn.

e13dc2010183a3b9: WASHINGTON: A lawyer for CNN, MS NOW and Politico urged a US federal judge on Wednesday to immediately restore White House access for the news organisations after President Donald Trump abruptly revoked their credentials.
District Judge Timothy Kelly declined to issue an immediate decision after a nearly one-hour court hearing but told lawyers for the media outlets and the government he would rule "as soon as I can."
CNN, MS NOW and Politico went to court after Trump on Friday ordered that they be barred from the White House as punishment for distributing what he called "fake news" and "fiction and lies."

The news organisations filed a lawsuit asking for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.
The Department of Justice responded with a court filing that said Trump can "control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office."
"Access to the White House is a privilege – not a right," it said.

In an accompanying letter to CNN, the White House Press Office accused the cable news network of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."
Similar accusations were levelled against MS NOW and Politico.

The letter to CNN cited several stories about the Iran war and a story on Trump's plans to build a military bunker below the planned East Wing ballroom which allegedly "disclosed 'top-secret' construction details."

Theodore Boutrous, representing the media outlets in court on Wednesday, told the judge that in his Truth Social post on Friday announcing the bans on CNN, MS NOW and Politico, Trump "didn't say anything about national security."
"All of a sudden this is a national security case," Boutrous said.

"The idea that reporters could be punished by the government simply for reporting on national security issues... that the government would rather have not been reported on is just contrary to First Amendment principles," he added.
'Trump TV'

Journalists for the three news organisations were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated in the latest flare-up of the 80-year-old Republican president's years-long assault on the mainstream US media.
In a previous case involving CNN during Trump's first term, Kelly, a Trump appointee, ordered the White House to temporarily restore White House access for a CNN reporter whose pass had been revoked.

In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters said on Monday that they were halting pool coverage of the White House – where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day – in solidarity with CNN.

"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said.
On Tuesday, Trump appeared to suggest that CNN should not be covering him outside of the White House too.
"I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me. You shouldn't be here," Trump told a CNN reporter at the UN General Assembly in New York.
On Monday evening, the White House launched a streaming channel, "Trump TV," which it said would show "top videos, major remarks, and must-see highlights streaming 24/7 and updated in real time."

The billionaire former reality TV star has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."

But the ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections, and the Iran war drags on with no end in sight.
